title: Reduce tracer mutex contention via per-request encoder pools and lockless sampling fast path
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: tracer encoder and sampling logic are contending on a global mutex in the hot request path. At high QPS (>20k), we observe significant CPU spikes and tail latency regressions caused by mutex contention and allocation churn from per-span encoding. Existing tail-based sampling runs on the hot path and requires quick decisions; the lock and allocation overhead amplify during burst traffic.

Goal: eliminate the global mutex from the hot path and reduce per-request tracer CPU and allocation cost by >40%, and reduce 99th percentile request CPU time for services using tracing by at least 30%. Ensure functional parity for sampling decisions (tail-based heuristics preserved) and add safe fallbacks.

Proposed design summary: 1) Introduce a small pooled set of per-request encoders (encoder pool) that are acquired from a bounded lock-free freelist to avoid blocking when contention is light and backpressure when saturated. 2) Implement a lockless fast-path for sampling decisions: use an atomic snapshot of current sampling config + precomputed predicates to make quick yes/no decisions without acquiring locks. 3) Move expensive tail-sampling heuristics to an asynchronous worker queue: the hot path records lightweight indicators (duration, error flag, tags) and enqueues candidate spans for background evaluation when needed. 4) Provide instrumentation and health metrics for the pool (borrow/return latencies, pool saturation), sampling fast-path hit-rate, and async worker backlog. 5) Feature-flag rollout and granular runtime knobs (pool size, queue length, sync fallback threshold).

Why different from prior work: prior tickets focused on tail-based sampling strategy or offloading to background workers in isolation. This ticket targets the specific root cause: a mutex around the encoder/sampler combined with allocation churn. The combined approach (pool + lockless fast-path + async heuristics) minimizes both lock and allocation overhead and keeps sampling quality comparable.

Acceptance criteria (high level): 1) Hotpath allocs per request from tracer reduced by >=40% in internal benchmark. 2) CPU cost attributable to tracer in our service benchmark reduced by >=30% at 50k QPS simulated. 3) No regression in sampling quality for existing eval prompt sets (false positives/negatives within 3% of baseline). 4) All new metrics emitted and visible in the observability dashboard. 5) Gradual canary rollout with automated rollback on defined SLO breach.

Implementation notes: - Implement the encoder pool as an MPMC lock-free freelist with hazard-refcounts for safe reclamation. Fallback to a bounded blocking allocation path when pool exhausted. - Sampling config updates will use copy-on-write atomic pointers to a precompiled predicate object to avoid locks on config reads. - Async evaluator uses a bounded ring buffer and a small worker pool; workers rehydrate minimal span info and run the full tail-sampling heuristics. - Add telemetry: tracer.encoder.borrow_ms, tracer.encoder.return_ms, tracer.pool.saturation, tracer.sampler.fastpath.hit_rate, tracer.async.queue_depth, tracer.async.dropped_count.

Rollout plan: merge behind feature flag. Canary on staging, then 5% production traffic for 24h, 25% for 48h, 100% if stable. Auto-rollback triggers: >10% increase in p95 latency or >5% increase in error rate for canary cohort.

Notes on safety: keep original mutex-protected path as a runtime-toggled fallback to ensure we can re-enable conservative behaviour if subtle correctness issues appear. Tests will include race detectors and long-running soak on a synthetic workload to catch leaks.

Links: design doc and bench run dashboards are attached below.
